flashcards.q: What's the difference between experiment tracking and a model registry?
flashcards.a: Tracking (MLflow/W&B) answers 'what code/params/data produced this run' -- reproducibility. A registry answers 'which artifact is approved for which environment right now' -- governance and promotion history.

flashcards.q: MLflow vs W&B: what's the real cost tradeoff?
flashcards.a: MLflow: Apache 2.0, free, self-hosted (~$150-500/mo infra) but you own ops burden. W&B: managed SaaS, Teams ~$50/user/mo, self-hosted enterprise only, ~$1.5-5K+/mo minimum. Verify current pricing before quoting.

flashcards.q: Why did MLflow deprecate stage-based model promotion (None/Staging/Production/Archived)?
flashcards.a: A version could hold only ONE stage, exclusive -- couldn't express a canary running alongside production, or two simultaneous A/B candidates. Replaced (MLflow 2.9+) with mutable, multi-assignable ALIASES (champion/candidate).

flashcards.q: Why version prompts the same way you version model weights?
flashcards.a: A one-line prompt wording change can shift output quality, safety behavior, and cost as much as a full model swap -- but unlike a model swap it's trivial to edit inline with zero review gate. Prompt registries add versioning, eval-gated promotion, and alias-based rollback.

flashcards.q: Architecturally, what's the difference between DVC and LakeFS?
flashcards.a: DVC: Git-adjacent, .dvc pointer files, COPY on checkout, ML-project scale. LakeFS: storage-native layer in front of an object store, branch/commit/merge as metadata ops, ZERO-COPY branching, data-lake scale for any consumer.

flashcards.q: What happened to DVC and LakeFS in November 2025?
flashcards.a: lakeFS acquired the DVC open-source project from Iterative.ai. DVC continues as the lightweight small-dataset tool; LakeFS continues as the enterprise-scale infrastructure layer, now under one company's roadmap.

flashcards.q: What does resolving `models:/name@champion` at serving load time buy you over hardcoding a version number?
flashcards.a: Promotion and rollback both become a single atomic alias reassignment in the registry, with zero code change and zero redeploy of the serving layer -- hardcoding couples model lifecycle to application deploy lifecycle unnecessarily.

flashcards.q: What full lineage chain does a registered model version need beyond just the artifact?
flashcards.a: Data version (DVC/LakeFS commit) -> code commit -> run ID with logged params/metrics -> registered version -> eval run that justified promotion -> alias/promotion history. The data-version link is the most commonly missing piece.

flashcards.q: Why is 'the pipeline didn't change' not the same claim as 'the data didn't change'?
flashcards.a: A pipeline reading a live source table can be byte-for-byte unchanged in code while the underlying data mutates (schema migration, backfill, new rows) between runs -- only an explicit immutable data version (DVC/LakeFS commit) closes this reproducibility gap.

flashcards.q: When is DVC the wrong tool, and when is LakeFS overkill?
flashcards.a: DVC is wrong at data-lake scale (multi-TB, multi-team) -- copy-on-checkout is too slow/expensive. LakeFS is overkill for a small single-team project's GB-scale train/test splits -- it's infrastructure overhead a Git-adjacent DVC workflow handles more simply.

flashcards.q: What governance gap does a prompt registry close that inline prompt strings can't?
flashcards.a: No version history, no diff, no eval gate, no rollback path beyond a full code revert+redeploy for an inline string. A prompt registry gives Git-like versioning, environment aliases, and eval-run linkage before promotion -- same discipline as a model registry.

flashcards.q: What can multiple aliases on the same model version express that a single stage field could not?
flashcards.a: E.g. a version tagged both `champion` and `stable-for-region-eu` simultaneously -- multiple simultaneous roles for one version, or two versions each holding a different alias (candidate vs champion) during a live A/B test -- structurally impossible with one exclusive stage field.
